name: swift-algorithms (min(count:), max(count:))
baseline: sorted().prefix(k) (sorting the whole collection to take the k smallest)
verdict_reason: The guide claims a speedup only when k is small and falls back to a full sort when k exceeds 10% of the collection, and its charts are consistent with that. The evidence is weak: the numbers exist only as chart images, collection size and machine are unstated, and the charts predate the fallback.
tier_reason: Numbers exist only in two chart images; the text gives complexity and the 10% cutoff, with no timings, hardware or toolchain.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in text. Complexity O(k log k + nk), close to O(n) for small k; falls back to sorting when k is more than 10% of the collection.
workload: Taking the k smallest elements of an Int collection for growing k, comparing a priority queue, the shipped SmallestM approach, a quicksort-based partial sort and Stdlib sort+prefix (charts, sizes unstated).
platforms: All Swift platforms: iOS, macOS, tvOS, watchOS, visionOS, Linux, Windows
one_liner: Apple's partial selection: the k smallest or largest elements in about O(n) for small k instead of sorting everything.
how_it_is_fast: min(count:) keeps a sorted buffer of the best k elements seen so far and skips any element larger than the current k-th, so most elements cost one comparison. That gives O(k log k + nk), which is near-linear when k is small, instead of O(n log n) for a full sort. Above 10% of the collection it switches to a full sort.
use_it_when: Top-N queries (top 10 scores, nearest 20 results) over large arrays
Code that calls sorted().prefix(k) or sorted().suffix(k) with k much smaller than n
Single-pass sequences, where sorting would need the whole sequence in memory anyway
skip_it_when: k is a large fraction of n: the function falls back to sorting anyway
You need the whole collection sorted later
caveats: Chart-only evidence (Guides/Resources/SortedPrefix/FewElements.png and ManyElements.png) with no stated collection size, hardware, build mode or Swift version.
The charts were made before the 10% fallback was added, so they show the shipped algorithm losing at large k.
Based on Soroush Khanlou's 2018 analysis, whose own speedup figures are theoretical or relative to his naive version, not to a full sort.
tradeoffs: Returns a new Array of k elements; no in-place partial sort
Worst case remains O(n log n) via the fallback

evidence.quote: The total complexity is `O(k log k + nk)`, which will result in a runtime close to `O(n)` if *k* is a small amount. If *k* is a large amount (more than 10% of the collection), we fall back to sorting the entire array.
